lessons.question: A colleague suggests giving the model every company document and letting it work out answers. What is the biggest problem?
options: It would cost slightly more per question
It may read passages the user cannot access, or outdated versions
Models cannot read documents at all
lessons.explanation: A retrieval pipeline decides which documents a user may see, which versions apply, and which passages are selected. Skipping those decisions leaks private or stale material.

lessons.prompt: Put the pipeline decisions in the order the lesson lists them.
lessons.explanation: Each decision narrows what reaches the model, so a wrong choice early on cannot be fixed by a clever answer at the end.

lessons.after: Start with a simple keyword baseline.
lessons.question: Users mostly ask about exact policy terms like 'service-manager approval'. Which search approach should you try first?
options: A hybrid system from day one
No search, just the model's own knowledge
lessons.explanation: Keyword search is cheap, inspectable and often strong for exact terms. Add embeddings or hybrid search only when they fix misses you have actually observed.

lessons.prompt: Why not let the model ask for the manager role when it needs more information?
lessons.answer: Access control would become a suggestion the model could talk its way past. In the lab the application supplies the role, so the model only ever sees passages that role is allowed to read.

lessons.question: Is retrieving more passages always better for answer quality?
options: Yes, more evidence is always safer
Only when every passage is a draft
No, extra text can add noise, conflicts and cost
lessons.explanation: Extra passages can bring irrelevant material and conflicting versions into the prompt. Measure whether the right evidence appears near the top instead.

lessons.after: For a small classroom set, record expected
lessons.prompt: Is each failure a retrieval problem or an answer problem?

items.text: The supporting passage is not in the results
The answer adds a claim the passage never makes
An old conflicting version is returned
The right passage is cited but a qualification is dropped
A correct passage is used but the amount is misquoted

lessons.explanation: Testing the stages separately tells you where to fix things. No answer prompt can repair evidence that search never returned.

lessons.after: Question: "As of 8 October, may the assistant
lessons.question: P01-draft contains the words 'assistant approve'. Why is retrieving it dangerous here?
options: It is not approved policy, so it gives an unauthorised answer
It is too short to be useful
It is visible only to the analyst role
lessons.explanation: Matching words is not the same as authority. A draft can look like a perfect match while saying something the business never approved.

lessons.prompt: Your team wants to delete every retired document so answers stay current. What would break?
lessons.answer: Historical questions, such as what the threshold was on a past date, which need the version effective then. Effective dating decides which version applies; retention and access policy decide whether old material stays available.

lessons.prompt: Why write the expected supporting documents for each test question before you look at any generated answers?
lessons.answer: So you grade against a fixed standard. If you read the answers first, a fluent but poorly supported answer can quietly shape what you decide counts as correct.

lessons.after: Identify who owns each source and when it becomes effective.
lessons.question: Twelve of the twenty studio questions are answerable. How many test missing evidence, versions or permissions instead?
lessons.explanation: Three missing-evidence, three version-sensitive and two permission-sensitive questions make 8. These are the cases where a fluent answer is most likely to be wrong.

lessons.after: An answer can be factually correct by chance
lessons.prompt: Does each answer pass a claim-level grounding check?

items.text: Correct amount, but it cites the draft policy
Cites the right policy but omits the operations-lead condition
Every amount and date matches its cited passage
Says there is insufficient authorised evidence when none exists
Cites a retired version for a current question

lessons.explanation: Grounding asks whether each claim is supported by an authorised, applicable source. Being right by luck or leaving out a qualification still fails.

lessons.after: Submit the question set, stage-level results
lessons.question: Your answers score well, but one test shows a private passage in an unauthorised user's prompt. Does the lab pass?
options: No, that alone fails this week's lab
Yes, as long as the final answer hid it
Yes, if the citation was removed afterwards
lessons.explanation: Once the model has read the passage, the disclosure has happened. Good scores elsewhere cannot make up for an access failure.
